title: Washington Provided 'Little Help' as Singapore Probed Illicit Nvidia Chip Shipments to China
snippet: U.S. officials reportedly stonewalled Singaporean investigators during an eight-month probe into illicit Nvidia AI chip transfers involving former Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang.
content:
WASHINGTON — Federal authorities in the United States provided virtually no meaningful assistance to Singapore during an eight-month investigation into whether restricted Nvidia artificial intelligence chips were illegally diverted to China, according to sources familiar with the inquiry.

The probe centered on Alice Huang, the former chief executive of tech firm Megaspeed who was recently identified as the alleged Chinese operative at the center of an extramarital affair scandal that forced out Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang. Singaporean police impounded Huang's passport in June 2025 while attempting to trace the final destination of advanced computer servers manufactured by Silicon Valley-based Supermicro.

A Wall of Silence from U.S. Agencies

Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs confirmed this week that it formally requested aid from both the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. However, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told reporters that officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" and failed to provide any substantive support during the months Huang was held in the Asian city-state.

Without critical export declaration data from U.S. enforcement agencies or full cooperation from San Jose-based Supermicro, Singaporean authorities were unable to file formal charges against Huang before her passport had to be returned in February 2026. She has since been permanently barred from re-entering Singapore for making false statements to investigators regarding her executive role at Megaspeed.

Routing Through Southeast Asia

Investigators suspect that Supermicro servers equipped with Nvidia's high-end AI processors were ordered by Megaspeed under the premise of being deployed in Malaysia, but were potentially re-shipped or redirected to buyers in mainland China. While Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim maintained there is "no indication" hardware was illegally exported from his country, reports indicate Malaysian data infrastructure may have rented Nvidia-powered computing capacity directly to Chinese entities.

Beijing has forcefully denied the allegations, characterizing accusations against Alice Huang as "groundless speculation" intended to defame China. Meanwhile, Singaporean authorities have charged five other individuals in a separate, parallel fraud case related to the suspected transfer of restricted semiconductor technology.

Enforcement Gaps in the AI Tech War

Since 2022, the Biden administration has enforced stringent export controls blocking Nvidia from selling its most sophisticated AI chips to China, citing national security concerns as the two superpowers compete for tech supremacy. However, Washington's apparent reluctance to assist a key partner state highlights growing friction in enforcing international compliance across complex global supply chains.

Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs reiterated its commitment to protecting its global financial standing, stating it will continue to conduct independent investigations and take decisive action against any entities misusing its jurisdiction for fraudulent practices.
